name: LTC3890EUH#TRPBF
title: LTC3890: 60V dual two-phase synchronous step-down DC/DC controller with 50µA quiescent current
summary: The LTC3890 is a two-channel synchronous buck controller that drives external N-channel MOSFETs from a 4V to 60V input and sets each output between 0.8V and 24V against a 0.8V reference. It uses constant-frequency peak current mode control with sensing by a resistor or the inductor DCR, and runs its two channels 180° apart to cut input ripple current. With one channel asleep in Burst Mode operation and the other off it draws 50µA; shut down it draws 14µA. Frequency is fixed at 350kHz or 535kHz, set by a resistor from 50kHz to 900kHz, or locked to a clock from 75kHz to 850kHz; it comes in a 5mm × 5mm 32-lead QFN.
key_figures: Quiescent current, sleep, one channel on
Maximum TG duty factor in dropout

notes: The E, I, H and MP grades are specified over different operating junction temperature ranges (Note 2 of the electrical table). All carry the marking 3890; a label on the shipping container identifies the grade.
The #W versions are built under controlled manufacturing for automotive use, and only these are for automotive applications.
A #TRMPBF suffix gives 500-unit reels for some packages. A 28-lead narrow SSOP version is a separate part, the LTC3890-1.

pins.name: SENSE1-
pins.function: Negative input of channel 1's differential current comparator. Above INTVCC – 0.5V this pin also supplies the comparator's current, about 700µA once it is above INTVCC + 0.5V.

pins.name: FREQ
pins.function: Sets the internal VCO frequency. Tied to GND: 350kHz. Tied to INTVCC: 535kHz. A resistor to GND programs 50kHz to 900kHz; an internal 20µA current into that resistor makes the control voltage.

pins.name: PHASMD
pins.function: Selects the phase of TG2 and CLKOUT relative to TG1. GND: 180° and 60°. Open: 180° and 90°. INTVCC: 240° and 120° (Table 1).

pins.name: CLKOUT
pins.function: Clock output for synchronizing further controllers in a multiphase chain; swings between ground and INTVCC.

pins.name: PLLIN/MODE
pins.function: Clock input to the phase detector and light-load mode select for both channels. With a clock applied, TG1's rising edge locks to the clock's rising edge. Without a clock: ground or open (internal 100k to ground) gives Burst Mode operation; INTVCC forces continuous inductor current; a level above 1.2V and below INTVCC – 1.3V gives pulse-skipping.

pins.name: SGND
pins.function: Small-signal ground shared by both controllers; route it apart from the high-current grounds to the common negative terminals of the input capacitors.

pins.name: RUN1
pins.function: Run control for channel 1. Below 1.16V channel 1 shuts down; with RUN2 also below 0.7V the whole IC shuts down to about 14µA. A 7µA internal pull-up lets the pin be left open to keep the channel on.

pins.name: RUN2
pins.function: Run control for channel 2. Below 1.20V channel 2 shuts down; with RUN1 also below 0.7V the whole IC shuts down. Internal pull-up is 0.5µA.

pins.name: SENSE2-
pins.function: Negative input of channel 2's differential current comparator; above INTVCC – 0.5V it also supplies the comparator's current.

pins.name: SENSE2+
pins.function: Positive input of channel 2's current comparator, normally taken to the sense resistor or a DCR sensing network. With ITH and the sense element it sets the current trip point.

pins.name: VFB2
pins.function: Feedback input of channel 2, from a resistor divider across the output.

pins.name: ITH2
pins.function: Error amplifier output and compensation node of channel 2; the current comparator's trip level rises with this voltage.

pins.name: TRACK/SS2
pins.function: Soft-start and tracking input of channel 2. VFB2 is regulated to the lower of 0.8V and this pin's voltage. A 1µA internal pull-up charges a capacitor to ground to set the ramp time; a divider from another supply makes the output track it.

pins.name: PGOOD2
pins.function: Power good for channel 2: pulled low when VFB2 is outside ±10% of its set point.

pins.name: TG2
pins.function: Gate drive for channel 2's top N-channel MOSFET, from a floating driver swinging INTVCC – 0.5V on top of SW2.

pins.name: SW2
pins.function: Switch node of channel 2, to the inductor.

pins.name: BOOST2
pins.function: Bootstrapped supply for channel 2's top-side driver: a capacitor to SW2 and a Schottky diode from INTVCC. Swings from INTVCC to VIN + INTVCC.

pins.name: BG2
pins.function: Gate drive for channel 2's bottom (synchronous) N-channel MOSFET; swings from ground to INTVCC.

pins.name: INTVCC
pins.function: Output of the internal low-dropout regulator that powers the drivers and control circuits. Decouple to power ground with at least 4.7µF of ceramic or other low-ESR capacitance; it is not for other loads.

pins.name: EXTVCC
pins.function: Input of a second internal LDO onto INTVCC. Above 4.7V it supplies INTVCC instead of the VIN regulator. Do not leave it open and do not exceed 14V.

pins.name: PGND
pins.function: Driver power ground, to the bottom MOSFET sources and the negative terminals of CIN.

pins.name: VIN
pins.function: Main supply input; bypass it to the signal ground pin.

pins.name: BG1
pins.function: Gate drive for channel 1's bottom (synchronous) N-channel MOSFET; swings from ground to INTVCC.

pins.name: BOOST1
pins.function: Bootstrapped supply for channel 1's top-side driver: a capacitor to SW1 and a Schottky diode from INTVCC. Swings from INTVCC to VIN + INTVCC.

pins.name: SW1
pins.function: Switch node of channel 1, to the inductor.

pins.name: TG1
pins.function: Gate drive for channel 1's top N-channel MOSFET, from a floating driver swinging INTVCC – 0.5V on top of SW1.

pins.name: PGOOD1
pins.function: Power good for channel 1: pulled low when VFB1 is outside ±10% of its set point.

pins.name: ILIM
pins.function: Three-level input setting the maximum current sense threshold of both comparators: SGND 30mV, INTVCC 50mV, open 75mV.

pins.name: TRACK/SS1
pins.function: Soft-start and tracking input of channel 1. VFB1 is regulated to the lower of 0.8V and this pin's voltage; 1µA internal pull-up.

pins.name: ITH1
pins.function: Error amplifier output and compensation node of channel 1; the current comparator's trip level rises with this voltage.

pins.name: VFB1
pins.function: Feedback input of channel 1, from a resistor divider across the output.

pins.name: SENSE1+
pins.function: Positive input of channel 1's current comparator, normally taken to the sense resistor or a DCR sensing network.

pins.name: SGND
pins.function: Exposed pad, connected to SGND; solder it to the PCB ground for the rated thermal performance.

notes: Pin 33 is the exposed pad on the underside.

circuits.title: High efficiency dual 8.5V/3.3V output step-down converter
circuits.description: Two synchronous buck outputs, 3.3V at 5A and 8.5V at 3A, from a 9V to 60V input. Each channel has its own top and bottom N-channel MOSFET, a bootstrap diode from INTVCC with a 0.1µF capacitor to the switch node, and a sense resistor between the inductor and the output that SENSE+ and SENSE– read. A 100k upper resistor with 31.6k or 10.5k below sets each output; a series 1000pF and 34.8k from ITH to ground compensates each loop, and 0.1µF on each TRACK/SS sets the start-up ramp.
notes: FREQ, PHASMD, CLKOUT, PLLIN/MODE, RUN1, RUN2, EXTVCC, PGOOD1, PGOOD2, ILIM and the exposed pad have no connection given in this circuit.

circuits.title: High efficiency dual 8.5V/3.3V step-down converter
circuits.description: The full dual buck behind the typical performance curves: 3.3V at 5A and 8.5V at 3A from 9V to 60V. Both channels use RJK0651DPB MOSFETs, DFLS1100 bootstrap diodes and resistor current sensing with a 1nF capacitor across each SENSE pair. RFREQ = 41.2k sets the frequency. EXTVCC takes the 8.5V output so the gate drive runs from it once it is up. ILIM, PHASMD, CLKOUT, PLLIN/MODE, RUN1 and RUN2 are left open: the 75mV sense range, Burst Mode operation and both channels enabled by their pull-up currents. Both PGOOD outputs pull up to INTVCC through 100k.

operation.text: Each channel is a constant-frequency peak current mode buck, and the two channels switch 180° apart. A clock pulse sets the channel's latch and turns on the top MOSFET; the current comparator ICMP resets it when inductor current reaches the peak level asked for by ITH, the error amplifier's output. The error amplifier compares VFB, taken from a divider across the output, with the 0.800V reference. A load increase pulls VFB slightly low, ITH rises, and average inductor current climbs to meet the load. After the top MOSFET turns off, the bottom MOSFET conducts until the next clock or until the reverse current comparator IR sees the inductor current about to reverse.

The gate drivers and most internal circuits run from INTVCC. With EXTVCC below 4.7V an LDO makes 5.1V on INTVCC from VIN; above 4.7V that LDO turns off and a second LDO makes 5.1V from EXTVCC, so INTVCC can come from an efficient source such as one of the converter's own outputs. The EXTVCC LDO stays on until EXTVCC falls below 4.5V. Each LDO can deliver 50mA peak. Bypass INTVCC with at least 4.7µF ceramic, and place an additional 1µF ceramic right at the INTVCC and PGND pins.

Each top driver runs from a bootstrap capacitor CB that recharges through an external diode while the top MOSFET is off. When VIN falls close to VOUT the loop would hold the top MOSFET on continuously; a dropout detector then forces it off for about one twelfth of a clock period every tenth cycle so CB can recharge. Maximum duty factor is 99% typ.

Pulling a RUN pin below about 1.15V stops that channel. With both RUN pins below 0.7V the IC turns off both channels and most internal circuits, the INTVCC LDOs included, and draws 14µA. Released, RUN1 is pulled up by 7µA and RUN2 by 0.5µA; the RUN1 current is large enough that the pin can be left open for a channel that is always on, without board leakage pulling it down. A RUN pin may be driven by logic up to the 8V absolute maximum, or connected through a resistor to a higher voltage such as VIN thanks to an internal 11V clamp, as long as the current into the pin stays at or below 100µA. PGOOD of a channel is held low while its RUN pin is low.

While TRACK/SS is below the 0.8V reference, VFB is regulated to the TRACK/SS voltage instead. A capacitor from TRACK/SS to SGND, charged by the internal 1µA source, makes a linear ramp from 0V up to 0.8V and on to 5V, and the output rises smoothly from zero to its set value. A resistor divider from another supply to TRACK/SS instead makes the output follow that supply during start-up, either coincidently (both rise together) or ratiometrically.

Burst Mode operation: PLLIN/MODE below 0.8V (for example SGND) or open. The peak inductor current is held at no less than about 25% of the maximum sense voltage. When load is light enough that ITH falls below 0.425V, the channel sleeps: both MOSFETs turn off, ITH is parked at 0.450V and much of the IC powers down, the output capacitor carries the load, and the IC draws 50µA with one channel asleep and the other off, or 60µA with both asleep. When the output sags far enough ITH reconnects and switching resumes on the next clock. Inductor current is not allowed to reverse. Forced continuous: PLLIN/MODE at INTVCC, or an external clock applied; inductor current may reverse, light-load efficiency is lower, and output ripple is low and independent of load, with less audio interference. Pulse-skipping: PLLIN/MODE between 1.2V and INTVCC – 1.3V; constant frequency down to about 1% of full load, then pulses are skipped, current is not allowed to reverse; ripple, audio noise and RF interference are lower than in Burst Mode operation and efficiency sits between the other two modes.

Lower frequency gives better efficiency through lower switching loss but needs more inductance and capacitance for the same ripple. Without an external clock, FREQ tied to SGND gives 350kHz, tied to INTVCC gives 535kHz, and a resistor from FREQ to SGND gives 50kHz to 900kHz (FREQ pin resistor curve). Table 2 lists the cases.

A clock on PLLIN/MODE is followed by a phase-frequency detector, a lowpass filter and the VCO, so controller 1's top MOSFET switches on at each rising clock edge; controller 2 turns on 180° later. The detector is edge sensitive with zero phase offset and does not lock to harmonics. The VCO input is pre-biased to the frequency set by FREQ, so setting FREQ near the clock frequency makes lock fast and keeps the frequency from sweeping widely while locking. The capture range is typically about 55kHz to 1MHz and is guaranteed from 75kHz to 850kHz. The clock input thresholds are typically 1.6V rising and 1.1V falling. At lock the detector stops driving its output and the internal capacitor CLP keeps the VCO voltage where it is.

CLKOUT provides a clock for further controllers in a multiphase supply feeding one high-current output or several outputs. PHASMD sets the phase of controller 2 and of CLKOUT relative to TG1's rising edge, per Table 1.

If VFB rises more than 10% above its 0.800V regulation point, the controller switches the top MOSFET off and holds the bottom MOSFET on for as long as the overvoltage lasts; normal operation then resumes by itself. This crowbar is meant to blow a system input fuse if the top MOSFET shorts while the controller runs. A leaky (not shorted) top MOSFET is handled by the loop trimming its duty cycle.

Each PGOOD pin is the open drain of an internal N-channel MOSFET, pulled low when its VFB is outside ±10% of 0.8V or its RUN pin is low, and released inside the window. Pull it up with a resistor to a supply of no more than 6V. A fault is reported after 25µs typ.

When the output falls below 70% of its nominal level, the maximum sense voltage is reduced progressively from 100% toward 45% of the selected value. Foldback is disabled during soft-start as long as VFB keeps up with TRACK/SS. In a short with very low duty cycle the controller begins skipping cycles; the bottom MOSFET then carries most of the dissipation, though less than in normal operation.

Running the two channels 180° apart interleaves their input current pulses, so the RMS current in the input capacitor drops; this allows cheaper input capacitors, less EMI shielding and better efficiency, and also lowers losses in the battery, fuse, switches and traces of the input path. In a measured 12V to 5V and 3.3V converter at 3A each, input RMS current fell from 2.53ARMS single-phase to 1.55ARMS two-phase, cutting the dissipation it causes by a factor of 2.66. The benefit depends on the channels' duty cycles; in most cases the input capacitor need only cover one channel at full current and 50% duty cycle, and the out-of-phase operation typically lowers capacitor ripple current by 30% to 70% against a single-phase design.

Either a low-value sense resistor or the inductor's DCR can be sensed. DCR sensing saves the resistor and its loss and is more efficient at high current; a resistor gives the most accurate current limit. Design proceeds from RSENSE and the inductor, then the MOSFETs and diodes, then the input and output capacitors.
ILIM is a three-level input setting the maximum sense threshold for both channels: grounded 30mV, open 75mV, tied to INTVCC 50mV.

The SENSE pins' common-mode range is 0V to 28V (absolute maximum), which allows nominal outputs up to 24V with margin. SENSE+ is high impedance over the whole range, drawing at most ±1µA, which suits DCR sensing. SENSE– draws under 1µA out of the pin below INTVCC – 0.5V and about 700µA into the pin above INTVCC + 0.5V, moving between the two in the band between. Place the filter parts close to the IC, run the two sense lines together to a Kelvin connection under the sense element, and in DCR sensing keep the resistor R1 close to the switch node so noise does not couple into small-signal nodes.

At duty cycles above 50% the internal slope compensation lowers the available peak current; the curve of maximum current sense threshold against duty cycle gives the reduction for very low dropout designs.

A DCR network can lose slightly more at light load than a sense resistor because of switching loss in R1, but it removes the resistor's conduction loss and wins at heavy load; peak efficiency is about the same either way.

Higher frequency allows smaller inductors and capacitors at the cost of MOSFET switching and gate charge loss. Larger ripple allows lower inductance but raises output ripple and core loss. Burst Mode operation begins when the needed peak current drops below 25% of the current limit, so lower inductance moves that transition to lower loads and lowers the burst frequency. Ferrite or molypermalloy cores suit high-efficiency designs; ferrite has low core loss at high frequency but saturates abruptly, so the core must not be allowed to saturate.

Each channel needs two N-channel MOSFETs, top and bottom. Gate drive comes from INTVCC (typically 5.1V at start-up), so logic-level threshold MOSFETs are needed in most designs; check BVDSS as well. Below about 20V input, larger MOSFETs generally improve high-current efficiency; above 20V transition losses rise quickly and a higher-RDS(ON) part with lower CMILLER can do better. The bottom MOSFET's loss peaks at high input with low duty cycle, or in a short circuit. Optional Schottky diodes across the bottom MOSFETs conduct in the dead time, stop the body diode from turning on and storing charge, and avoid a reverse recovery cost of up to 3% efficiency at high input voltage; a Schottky rated 1A to 3A suits both regions, as larger ones add switching loss through their capacitance.

Size CIN for the RMS current of the channel with the larger VOUT × IOUT with that channel running alone (Equation 1); load on the other channel only reduces it. Use a low-ESR capacitor; derate electrolytics (ripple ratings are often for only 2000 hours) or choose a higher temperature rating, parallel capacitors if needed, and ceramic capacitors can be used. Place the top MOSFET drains within 1cm of each other on a shared CIN; separating them can cause resonances at VIN. A 0.1µF to 1µF bypass from the VIN pin to ground close to the IC is suggested, and a 10Ω resistor between CIN and the VIN pin adds isolation between channels. COUT is chosen mainly by ESR; once that is met the capacitance is usually enough.
Place the feedback divider across the output and route the VFB trace away from noise sources such as the inductor and the switch node.

INTVCC current is dominated by gate charge and rises with frequency. When the VIN LDO supplies it, IC dissipation is VIN × IINTVCC, which with large MOSFETs at high frequency and high input can exceed the junction limit; check the input current in forced continuous mode at maximum VIN. While EXTVCC is below 5.1V its LDO is in dropout and INTVCC is about equal to EXTVCC; from 5.1V to the 14V maximum INTVCC is regulated to 5.1V. Supplying INTVCC from an output (4.7V ≤ VOUT ≤ 14V) scales the input current for drive and control by duty cycle over efficiency. For more current than the EXTVCC LDO provides, a Schottky diode may be added from EXTVCC to INTVCC; then keep EXTVCC at or below 6V and at or below VIN.

1. Grounded: INTVCC comes from the internal 5.1V regulator, costing up to 10% efficiency at high input voltage. 2. Directly to VOUT: the normal connection for a 5V to 14V output, giving the highest efficiency. 3. To an external 5V to 14V supply compatible with the gate drive, kept below VIN. 4. To a voltage derived from a low output (3.3V or less) and boosted above 4.7V by a capacitive charge pump (BAT85 diodes and an NDS7002), kept below VIN.

CB charges from INTVCC through DB while SW is low. To turn the top MOSFET on, the driver puts CB's voltage across its gate and source; SW rises to VIN and BOOST follows to VIN + VINTVCC. CB should be 100 times the total input capacitance of the top MOSFET(s), and DB's reverse breakdown must exceed VIN(MAX). DB may be Schottky or silicon but needs low leakage and fast recovery. For outputs above about 5V switching rarely (Burst Mode operation at very light load, where INTVCC draws only about 35µA), or after shutdown if CB discharges before the output falls below about 5V, DB leakage can make a path from the output through BOOST to INTVCC, raising quiescent current and possibly driving INTVCC to dangerous levels. In shutdown INTVCC can sink about 30µA; for more leakage load INTVCC with a resistor or Zener clamp, or let a PGOOD pull-up to INTVCC sink it — but choosing a diode with low leakage is preferred.
The ripple current in a short is set by the minimum on-time (about 95ns), the input voltage and the inductance; the average short-circuit current is 45% of the current limit minus half that ripple.

The minimum on-time, set by internal delays and the top MOSFET's gate charge, is about 95ns and rises toward about 130ns as the peak sense voltage falls; this matters most in forced continuous designs with low ripple at light load, where heavy cycle skipping with larger ripple can follow.

The main losses are: the IC's VIN current (typically under 0.1%); INTVCC current for gate drive and control, cut from 10% or more to a few percent by supplying INTVCC from an output through EXTVCC (in a 20V to 5V design, 10mA of INTVCC current becomes about 2.5mA from VIN); I²R losses in the fuse, MOSFETs, inductor, sense resistor and capacitor ESR (for example 130mΩ total gives 3% to 13% loss from 1A to 5A at 5V out, or 4% to 20% at 3.3V); and top MOSFET transition losses, significant at inputs of about 15V and up. Copper and battery resistance can add 5% to 10% in portable systems; a 25W supply typically needs at least 20µF to 40µF of input capacitance with at most 20mΩ to 50mΩ ESR. Dead-time diode conduction and core loss usually add under 2%.

Loop response can be checked with a load step: VOUT first moves by ∆ILOAD × ESR, then recovers; overshoot or ringing shows a stability problem. ITH is a DC-coupled, AC-filtered view of the closed loop, so its overshoot gives phase margin or damping and its rise time gives bandwidth, for a load pulse of 20% to 80% of full load with a 1µs to 10µs rise. The series RC on ITH sets the dominant pole-zero; values from 0.5 to 2 times those of the dual 8.5V/3.3V converter are a starting range once layout and output capacitors are fixed. Raising RC raises loop gain, lowering CC raises bandwidth, and changing both by the same factor keeps the zero in place. Switching in a load with more than 1:50 of COUT as bypass capacitance needs its rise time limited to about 25 • CLOAD (a 10µF load gives 250µs and about 200mA).

One channel, VIN = 12V nominal and 22V maximum, VOUT = 3.3V, IMAX = 5A, VSENSE(MAX) = 75mV, f = 350kHz (FREQ to GND). A 4.7µH inductor gives 29% ripple and a 5.73A peak. The on-time at maximum input is 3.3V / (22V × 350kHz) = 429ns, well above 95ns. With the 64mV minimum threshold, RSENSE ≤ 64mV / 5.73A ≈ 0.01Ω. RA = 25k and RB = 78.7k (1%) give 3.32V. An FDS6982S dual MOSFET (RDS(ON) = 0.035Ω/0.022Ω, CMILLER = 215pF) at 22V and 50°C gives PMAIN = 331mW. A short gives ISC = 34mV / 0.01Ω – ½ × (95ns × 22V / 4.7µH) = 3.18A, and the bottom MOSFET then dissipates PSYNC = (3.28A)² × 1.125 × 0.022Ω = 250mW. CIN needs at least 3A RMS rating with this channel alone; COUT with 0.02Ω ESR gives about 0.02Ω × 1.45A = 29mVP-P ripple.

1. Keep the two top MOSFETs no more than 1cm apart, their drains joined at CIN; do not split the input decoupling between channels. 2. Keep signal and power grounds apart: the IC signal ground and CINTVCC's return go to the combined COUT negative terminals; keep the loop of top MOSFET, Schottky and CIN short; put the COUT negative terminals next to the CIN negative terminals, away from that loop. 3. Connect each VFB divider between COUT's positive terminal and signal ground, not along the input current paths. 4. Route SENSE+ and SENSE– together at minimum spacing with the filter capacitor close to the IC and Kelvin connections at the sense resistor. 5. Place the INTVCC capacitor close to the IC between INTVCC and PGND; an extra 1µF right at those pins helps noise considerably. 6. Keep SW, TG and BOOST nodes away from small-signal nodes, especially the other channel's sense and feedback pins, on the output side of the IC with minimum area. 7. Use a modified star ground: one low-impedance copper area on the capacitors' side of the board, with the INTVCC capacitor, the feedback dividers and SGND tied into it.

Test one controller at a time with a current probe on the inductor, triggering on SW. The frequency should hold over the input range down to dropout and down to the light-load threshold (typically 15% of maximum current in Burst Mode operation), and duty cycle should be steady from cycle to cycle; subharmonic variation points to noise at the sense inputs or poor compensation. Duty cycle jitter can appear near 50% duty when one channel nears its trip point as the other turns on. Problems at high input and low load suggest capacitive coupling from BOOST, SW, TG or BG into sense pins; problems at high load and low input suggest inductive coupling from CIN, the Schottky and the top MOSFET. Reversed sense leads still regulate but lose the benefits of current mode control; shorting the sense resistor briefly shows this.
